column3: Known as the first iron bridge on the Yellow River, it was built in 1909 and is now a walking bridge in the heart of Lanzhou.
A hill on the north bank of the Yellow River with a white pagoda on top. Stairs and pavilions lead up to a view over the city and the river.
A calm stone mother sits by the river with a laughing baby, a symbol of the Yellow River as the mother river of China.
The museum holds the Flying Horse of Gansu, a Han bronze horse with one hoof on a swallow, and many treasures from the Silk Road.
A park on the slope of a hill south of Lanzhou, with springs, old temples and gardens, a quiet place away from the busy city.
Hand-pulled noodles in clear beef broth with a bright chili oil, green coriander, white radish and yellow noodles. Locals eat it for breakfast and it is a symbol of Lanzhou.
Mutton boiled with simple spices until tender, then picked up with the hands and eaten with salt or garlic sauce. It is a classic way to eat in northwest China.
Cool, springy noodles made from wheat or rice starch, tossed with chili oil, vinegar and sesame. Perfect for a hot day.
Lanzhou lily bulbs are sweet and not bitter, and are famous in China. They are cooked in soups or eaten as a sweet snack.
A sweet drink made by fermenting oats or barley. Its taste is gently sweet with a touch of wine and cools you on a warm day.
A warm sweet dessert of pea beans stewed with sugar and spices, a street treat in winter in Lanzhou.
Hundreds of cave temples carved into a desert cliff over a thousand years, filled with Buddhist murals and statues. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a treasure of the Silk Road.
Huge golden dunes outside Dunhuang that are said to make a sound when the sand moves. Visitors climb the ridge or ride camels.
A crescent-shaped spring that has been surrounded by dunes for thousands of years and has never dried up, a rare green oasis.
A Han-dynasty frontier pass at the edge of the desert, once the gateway to the West and sung about in many poems.
A pass south of Dunhuang that was another gate to the Silk Road. Travelers crossing it left their homeland and entered the unknown.
A small hidden cave at Mogao in which more than 50,000 scrolls and documents were found in 1900, a priceless record of life along the Silk Road.
Yellow noodles, made with alkaline water, served with slices of braised donkey meat, a savory and filling dish in Dunhuang.
A cold drink of dried apricot peel, sugar and herbs. It is sweet, sour and very refreshing in the dry heat of the desert.
A sweet apricot grown in Dunhuang's oasis, named after the Han general Li Guang, and ripe in early summer.
Paintings on the cave walls tell Buddhist tales and show daily life, music and dance. Some of the colors have lasted for more than a thousand years.
Graceful flying figures in the Mogao murals, with ribbons streaming behind them. They have become a symbol of Dunhuang.
A famous pose from the Dunhuang murals, in which a dancer plays the pipa behind her back while she dances. It is an emblem of Dunhuang art.
A great Ming fortress at the western end of the Great Wall, with strong gates and towers. In the past it marked the edge of the empire.
A section of the Great Wall that climbs a very steep ridge at an angle near Jiayuguan, and is rebuilt after the Ming dynasty.
Skewered or roasted mutton cooked over fire with cumin and chili is a staple of an evening in the northwest.
A round flatbread baked in an oven until golden and crisp, often eaten with mutton or soup.
Hills striped in red, orange, yellow and white, like a painted landscape. Colors glow in the light of the evening, and it is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The popular name for the rainbow-colored hills of Zhangye, where thin layers of different minerals have been shaped by wind and rain.
A group of cave temples in the Qilian foothills, near a rock where a horse is said to have left a hoofprint.
Short noodles rolled by hand into tapered fish shapes and served with a savory sauce, a favorite in Zhangye.
Tender braised meat tucked into a baked bun, a northwest classic enjoyed all over Gansu.
Cave temples carved on a lone cliff that looks like a haystack. Hundreds of caves hold clay statues with gentle smiles. It is part of the Silk Road UNESCO site.
A temple to Fuxi, a mythical ancestor who taught people to fish and drew the eight trigrams. It is a grand ancient hall in Tianshui.
A cold dish of soft buckwheat jelly, served with chili oil, vinegar and garlic, a street snack of Tianshui.
Noodles made from buckwheat, served in a savory soup or with a spicy sauce. They taste earthy and slightly sweet.
A cave temple complex on the Yellow River, reached by boat across a reservoir, with a giant Buddha carved into the cliff.
Dumplings baked in a hot oven until the skin is crisp and the mutton filling is juicy, a common treat in Linxia.
Linxia is famous for its carved brick work, with fine flowers and landscapes cut by hand on gateways and screen walls.
A mountain of temples and cliffs that is famous in Taoism and martial arts stories as a place where masters trained.
A chicken cooked slowly with spices until it falls apart, a well-known local dish.
China's first space launch center in the Gobi desert, where its crewed spaceflights take off.
Thin cups carved from local green jade, said to glow at night. A poem from the Tang dynasty made them famous.
Grilled lamb seasoned with cumin and salt, with a smoky aroma, a typical dish of the desert oasis.
Wudu in Longnan is a rare place in China where olives grow, and its olive oil is a regional specialty.
A famous Sichuan pepper from Wudu, with a strong fragrance and a tingling taste that fills many Chinese dishes.
One of the six great monasteries of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, with golden roofs, prayer wheels and monks in red.
A small town on the Gansu-Sichuan border with two monasteries, a river and green hills. Tibetans, Hui and Han people live here together.
A wide, high grassland where yaks and sheep graze under big skies. Tibetan tents and wildflowers dot the summer pastures.
Thick yogurt made from yak milk, tangy and rich, often eaten with sugar or tsampa on the plateau.
Roasted barley flour that is mixed with butter tea into a dough and eaten by hand, a daily staple for Tibetan herders.
